queue.title: Amtrak ridership hits record as high gas prices drive more Americans to train travel

queue.opening: Amtrak said this week that it hit a record 37.1 million riders over the past year, a 7.4% jump fueled in part by Americans ditching expensive flights and high gas prices. The company posted an adjusted net loss of $492.7 million — a 19% improvement over the previous year. It marks the third straight year of record-breaking passenger volume for the rail operator. "I have no doubt that the airline prices, gas prices pushed people to say, 'Maybe I should ride the train instead'," interim President Byl Herrmann said in an interview. Amtrak plans to replace its Northeast regional trainsets by 2028 and last year began replacing its higher-speed Acela trains with new trainsets. "Frankly, I want to be in a range where I'm competing with the airlines, and some of these airlines, we're going to surpass them in the next few years for the number of passengers they have," Herrmann said. queue.dek: Dr. Joel Davis Brown says swapping "yes, but" for "yes, and" can keep Thanksgiving dinner talk civil as post-midterm politics turn tense at the table.
queue.opening: As Americans across the country sit down to Thanksgiving dinner just weeks after Democrats' midterm sweep drastically reshaped the political landscape going into 2027, conversations about politics and the economy could turn tense. Dr. Joel Davis Brown, a leadership expert, executive coach and author who studies how people communicate and navigate conflict, says swapping out the word "but" when discussing controversial topics can help keep the discussions civil. "‘But’ shows disagreement," Brown told Fox News Digital. "It’s a way of telling the person that what they said should not be heard, and it really stifles conversation." Instead, Brown suggests trying "yes, and." That doesn’t mean you have to agree, he said. Rather, it signals that you’ve heard the other person and leaves room to share a different view. "‘Yes, I’ve heard you and I have a different opinion,’" Brown said. "We can listen to varying opinions." FOOD PRICES ARE RISING BEFORE THANKSGIVING. AN ECONOMIST SHARES WAYS TO SAVE If a hot-button topic comes up, Brown recommends asking the person to "tell me more about that." The question, he says, can help you understand how someone arrived at their view instead of turning the exchange into a debate. He also cautions against opening with "I disagree," which can put people "in an oppositional place" before they have fully heard one another.
